# Vue — reactivity, component contracts, cleanup, and universal rendering

Read this for Vue UI code. The universal frontend rules live in `skills/frontend-craft/SKILL.md`,
and the universal TypeScript language rules live in the `language-idiom` skill loaded alongside it.
On any conflict, those owners and the target repository win.

## Contents

- Establish the Vue contract
- Reactivity is explicit ownership
- Props, events, models, and slots

## Establish the Vue contract

- Read the target package's `package.json`, lockfile, Vue compiler and runtime versions, framework
  configuration, and build plugins first. The runtime and `@vue/compiler-sfc` must be compatible;
  a workspace-root dependency does not prove the touched package uses it.
- Determine whether the target is a client-rendered SPA, SSR/hydrated, statically generated, or a
  mixture. Also identify the repository's Options API or Composition API conventions and whether
  it uses `<script setup>`.
- Match the established router, store, data-fetching, form, styling, and test layers. Adding a Vue
  component is not authority to migrate API styles, introduce a store, or replace those layers.
- Treat version-sensitive compiler behavior as part of the contract. Vue 3.4 and 3.5 differ in
  computed stability, reactive props destructuring, watcher cleanup, hydration, and other APIs.

## Reactivity is explicit ownership

- Use `ref` for an independently replaceable value and `reactive` for an object whose proxy
  identity remains stable. Access refs with `.value` in JavaScript; template unwrapping and nested
  unwrapping have specific rules, so do not infer runtime shape from template syntax.
- Do not destructure properties from an ordinary `reactive` object when the destructured binding
  must remain reactive. Keep property access through the proxy or use the repository's established
  `toRef`/`toRefs` pattern.
- **Use `computed` for pure derived values.** A computed getter must not mutate other state, make
  network requests, write the DOM, or start timers. Use a watcher only for an actual side effect.
- Keep state minimal and mutations close to its owner. When using provide/inject, expose
  intentional actions from the provider rather than letting distant consumers mutate shared state
  arbitrarily. Use a store only when the repository's ownership boundary genuinely needs one.
- Replace or mutate reactive collections according to the chosen primitive. Reassigning a
  `reactive` variable to a new object disconnects consumers of the old proxy; a `ref` is the
  clearer choice when whole-value replacement is part of the contract.
- Keys identify list items and component instances. Use stable domain identity, not array position
  or randomness, when items can reorder, insert, or preserve local state.

## Props, events, models, and slots

- Props are one-way and readonly in the child. Derive a transformed view with `computed`, or
  initialize deliberately independent local state when the prop is only an initial value.
- Nested objects and arrays passed as props can still be mutated because preventing deep mutation
  would be expensive. Avoid that hidden parent mutation unless parent and child are intentionally
  tightly coupled; normally emit an event or invoke an owned action.
- Declare props and emitted events, including payload types. Component events do not bubble through
  the component tree, so a distant owner needs explicit forwarding or shared state—not an assumed
  DOM-style event chain.
- Implement `v-model` through the repository's Vue-version-compatible model contract. Do not mutate
  the incoming model prop; emit the corresponding update event.
- Slots are caller-owned structure. Keep slot props small and typed, provide accessible defaults
  where useful, and do not hide required behavior in implicit slot scope.
- Fallthrough attributes and listeners can land on an unintended root when a component changes
  shape. For multi-root or wrapper components, forward `$attrs` deliberately and test the rendered
  focus, ARIA, class, and listener targets.
- In Vue 3.5+, destructured variables from `defineProps` are compiler-rewritten as reactive within
  the same `<script setup>` block. Before 3.5 they do not have that behavior. Even on 3.5+, pass a
  getter such as `() => foo` to `watch`; passing the current value is not a reactive source.

## Watchers and lifecycle cleanup

- Use `watch` when the dependency list and old/new values matter. Use `watchEffect` for a concise
  side effect whose synchronous reactive reads define its dependencies. In an async
  `watchEffect`, only reads before the first `await` are tracked.
- Cancel or retire stale asynchronous work when a watcher invalidates. The callback's `onCleanup`
  argument is bound to that watcher and works across supported Vue 3 releases. Vue 3.5+
  `onWatcherCleanup` must be registered synchronously before an `await`; do not emit it for an
  older target.
- Watchers declared synchronously during component setup are stopped with their owner. A watcher
  created later in an asynchronous callback is not automatically owned; retain and call its stop
  handle, or structure setup so the watcher exists synchronously and gates on readiness.
- Side effects that require browser resources start in client-only lifecycle hooks and undo their
  work in `onUnmounted`: remove listeners, disconnect observers and sockets, clear timers, abort
  requests, and dispose third-party widgets.
- Watchers run according to their configured flush timing. If a side effect must observe Vue's
  updated DOM, use the narrow established `flush: "post"` or `nextTick` pattern. Do not turn
  timing options into a substitute for clear data flow.
- Keep composables synchronous during component setup when they depend on the active component
  instance. Return a plain object of refs when consumers may destructure it, and keep cleanup in
  the composable that acquired the resource.

## Errors and asynchronous UI

- Use `onErrorCaptured`/`errorCaptured` at a meaningful descendant boundary for local handling and
  `app.config.errorHandler` for final uncaught application reporting. A global logger alone does
  not provide the designed per-panel fallback the Resilience UX rules require.
- Returning `false` from an error-capture hook stops further propagation; do it only when that
  boundary has actually handled the failure. Avoid rendering the same failing content in the
  fallback path and causing a loop.
- Vue has no exact built-in equivalent to React's Error Boundary component. `<Suspense>`
  coordinates supported asynchronous dependencies; it is not a general error boundary.
- Keep async loading, empty, error, retry, and stale-result behavior explicit. Prefer the
  repository's router loader or query/cache layer for server state over ad hoc watchers that
  duplicate caching, cancellation, and request ownership.

## SSR and hydration

- Universal render code must not assume `window`, `document`, or a browser-only API exists. Start
  effects needing cleanup in mounted client lifecycle, because unmount hooks do not run for
  server-only work.
- Create fresh app, router, store, and request state for every SSR request. Module-scope singleton
  state can leak one user's data into another request.
- The server and first client render must be deterministic. Random values, current time,
  timezone/locale differences, invalid HTML, and environment branches cause hydration mismatches;
  pass stable inputs or defer truly client-only output until mounted.
- Treat hydration mismatches as bugs. Vue 3.5+ `data-allow-mismatch` is a narrow escape hatch for
  an intentionally unavoidable difference, not a general repair mechanism.
- Values serialized into hydration state are visible to the client. Do not include secrets or
  unsafe executable markup, and use the target framework's serialization contract rather than
  embedding raw JSON into HTML without escaping.

## Security boundaries

- Never compile user-controlled content as a Vue template. Templates execute in the application's
  context and cannot be made safe merely by escaping interpolated values.
- Text interpolation and ordinary dynamic attributes are escaped, but `v-html` and direct DOM HTML
  insertion are not sanitizers. Use them only for content accepted by an explicitly owned
  sanitization policy.
- Validate user-controlled URLs before binding or navigating. Sanitize URL inputs on the server
  where possible, allowlist user-controlled style properties, and never render user-provided
  JavaScript.
- Client route guards and hidden controls are usability boundaries, not authorization. Enforce
  identity, object access, and mutation policy again at the server boundary.

## Performance and testing

- Measure with browser tooling and Vue's performance instrumentation before optimizing. Reduce
  unnecessary work by keeping child props stable and state local before adding memoization hints.
- Lazy-load routes and genuinely heavy features not needed initially. Use list virtualization for
  measured large collections; do not render thousands of hidden rows and call pagination solved.
- `v-once` is for permanently static content. Use `v-memo` or shallow reactivity only for measured
  large-tree or large-data bottlenecks, with tests proving the immutable update discipline they
  require.
- Computed dependency stability improved in Vue 3.4. Do not prescribe manual old-value optimization
  without checking the installed version and profiling the actual dependency path.
- Test observable component behavior: rendered accessibility, props, emitted events, slots,
  lifecycle cleanup, and user interactions. Avoid asserting private refs or mocking every child.
- Use real-browser coverage for router behavior, global state, hydration, focus, asset loading, and
  network integration. A shallow component test does not prove those contracts.

## Verify

Run the target package's declared typecheck, lint, unit/component tests, production build, and
browser flow. Record the Vue/compiler versions, API style, and whether the exercised path was
client-only, server-rendered, or hydrated. When watcher or lifecycle ownership changes, prove stale
work is cancelled and all acquired resources are released.
